They are not so in an ultimate sense, for even when one sees everything that resides therein, all conventional designations are absent. By this, the subduing of distraction is taught.If there is no phenomenon whatsoever that the Tathāgata has perfectly realized, then how can a bodhisattva take up the instructions and realize the selflessness of phenomena and persons? Thinking this, the statement beginning with "Just as, for example..." was spoken to demonstrate realization. This teaches realization through the attainment of primordial wisdom and the absence of pride. What is the nature of this attained primordial wisdom? It relies on two types of primordial wisdom: the primordial wisdom that fully grasps the lineage, and the primordial wisdom of equality. Among these, the primordial wisdom that fully grasps the lineage is that which, once attained, causes one to be born into the lineage of the Tathāgata and be certain of the lineage of the Buddha. By being born of it, one possesses a body. "Possessing" means that which is made one's own; the "body" is the body of the Tathāgata, and whoever attains that possesses the body. Thinking, "How is it known that this primordial wisdom is attained?" the phrase "great body" was spoken. By this, it is shown that having attained the primordial wisdom of equality through the selflessness of persons and phenomena, one realizes [the truth]; therefore, it is taught as the primordial wisdom of the lineage. Through that primordial wisdom of equality, one realizes that all sentient beings are selfless in terms of persons and phenomena, and thus one gathers them into the self alone. Therefore, because it gathers the bodies of all sentient beings into the self, it is a "great body." This is not merely a literal meaning, for in this way, because all sentient beings are gathered into the self, it is called a "body." And because they are extremely numerous, it is a "great body," so it is not merely a literal meaning. By this, the vastness of this state is expressed.The intention is this: the realization of a Bodhisattva is distinguished merely by the arising of superior primordial wisdom that relies upon valid conventional reality; in the ultimate sense, however, there is neither a realizer nor anything to be realized. To teach this, the noble Subhūti addressed the Tathāgata, saying, "The Tathāgata possesses a human body," and so forth. By this, he indicates in essence the discordant factor of being attached to having a body and a great body. In order to abandon that, he teaches that one should abide through aspiration and prayer.By stating "possessing a body and a great body," he merely expresses a sign, through which he causes the Bodhisattva to turn away from attachment to all phenomena. He also establishes them in the ultimate sense, and he leads them into meditative equipoise in that. He also expresses the profound. He also abandons the extreme of superimposition. By the former, he has blocked the extreme of denigration. If the Tathāgata were to teach that that very body does not exist, then, at that time, those Bodhisattvas who have attained realization might think, "Since I have attained the realization of a Bodhisattva, I shall now liberate sentient beings." Because they lack the pride of realization, having examined the noble conceptualization of others, he spoke the words "what is a Bodhisattva" in order to teach realization.This shows that one who thinks, "I shall liberate sentient beings," and who thinks, "I am a Bodhisattva," is, in the ultimate sense, not a Bodhisattva, because they possess the pride of realization. The phrase "For what reason?" is an inquiry into the logical grounds for understanding this here. The term "phenomena" refers to the nature of form and so forth, or the nature of the person and so forth. The noble Subhūti also replied, "They do not exist," because when those phenomena are examined through reasoning, they are not seen. Since that reasoning is common to both, the Blessed One spoke the words "Therefore" in order to establish the lack of self in both. The phrase "no sentient beings" and so forth is an indication; one should also view them as lacking intrinsic nature. By this, the subduing of mental wandering is taught. The realization has been explained.From this point onward is the investigation of the Buddha, and that Buddha is also comprised of seven perfections. The seven perfections are: the perfection of the completely pure field, the perfection of the completely pure unsurpassed vision, the perfection of the completely pure unsurpassed knowledge, the perfection of the mastery of the accumulation of merit, the perfection of the body, the perfection of speech, and the perfection of the mind.In this regard, if there were any such entity called a bodhisattva, then who would strive to accomplish the purification of a buddha-field? To dispel such doubts, and focusing on the perfection of the completely pure buddha-field, he spoke the words beginning with, "Subhūti, whatever bodhisattva..." The phrase "one should speak in that way" is intended to mean that one should not say, "This is a bodhisattva," because of the presence of conceit; it is because one engages in conceit, thinking that one has realized the non-self of persons and phenomena when one has not. In this way, by thinking "I am," one has not realized the non-self of persons. By engaging in conceit regarding the buddha-fields, thinking they exist when they do not, one has not realized the non-self of phenomena. This teaches how a bodhisattva should abide by having faith that the buddha-fields are like an illusion. If, in the ultimate sense, those buddha-fields did not exist, one might wonder how the Blessed One could have spoken of them; thus, the question "Why is that?" is asked, and the explanation for this is as before. This does not result in a repetition of words, for the former was to dispel the conceptualizations of a bodhisattva who is abiding on the stage of engaging through faith, at the time when he is aspiring for the purification of a bodhisattva-field. Now, it is taught in order to dispel the conceptualizations of those who, when entering upon the path to accomplish the purification of a buddha-field, think that they are entering with such attachment. At that time, because such conceptualizations do not arise in others, it does not result in an infinite regress. This teaches how a bodhisattva should accomplish this.Thinking, "What kind of being is called a bodhisattva?" the text states, "Subhūti, whatever bodhisattva..." and so forth. The fact that "phenomena are selfless" is stated twice indicates that phenomena are shown to be selfless by way of the two types of selflessness. The fact that "bodhisattva, mahāsattva" is stated twice indicates that one realizes those very two types of selflessness. Alternatively, one instance of "bodhisattva" is a repetition. The subsequent phrase, "it is called a bodhisattva," is the method. Therefore, how is it explained? It will be shown that they are called bodhisattvas because they have understood both the absence of grasping at a person and the like, thinking "by whom will it be accomplished," and the absence of grasping at the "array of buddha-fields" as a phenomenon. By this, the firm grasping of the mind is shown. By all of this, profundity is shown. Because it is shown that bodhisattvas engage with faith in order to accomplish those buddha-fields which are like illusions, vastness is expressed.If there were any phenomenon whatsoever called a "bodhisattva," then at that time, the Tathāgata would be devoid of perfectly pure vision and devoid of perfectly pure knowledge. For if that which is born from the bodhisattva does not exist, how could that [Tathāgata] be possible? To be without a cause would result in the meaning of being eternally existent and so forth.Therefore, for the sake of the gathered assembly who might conceive of such thoughts, the Tathāgata, having regard for the two supreme, perfectly pure [faculties of] vision and knowledge, spoke [the words] beginning with, "Subhūti, what do you think?" The noble Subhūti also, having grasped the intent of the Blessed One beforehand, replied, "I have [understood]." This [passage] indicates that although, in the ultimate sense, there is no phenomenon whatsoever called a "bodhisattva," there is, in the conventional sense, the existence of a bodhisattva who is merely a nature of aggregates, which is a delight when not analyzed in isolation, [and who] having fulfilled the accumulations of merit and wisdom, becomes a Tathāgata whose knowledge and vision are perfectly pure. It is not otherwise; for if that [bodhisattva] did not exist even conventionally, then who would become a Tathāgata? Thus, it teaches that. Regarding that, the statement that the Tathāgata possesses only the eye of wisdom is not made; rather, it teaches that he possesses the eye in order to show that his perfectly pure vision has reached excellence. In summary, there are four types of eyes: the eye that perceives form, the eye that perceives the ultimate truth, the eye that perceives the conventional truth, and the eye that perceives all knowable things in every aspect. The eye that perceives form is also of two types: the result of action and the result of cultivation. [These correspond] to the five types of eyes in their respective order. Among these, because the object is coarse, the eye that perceives form is taught first. Because of the power of the ultimate, conventional knowledge becomes perfectly pure; therefore, the eye that perceives the ultimate truth is taught first, and the eye that perceives the conventional truth is explained later—this is the connection that shows the order.The eye of wisdom exists regarding the object of the selflessness of persons and phenomena. Because the person is not, but rather it is merely the appearance of phenomena in conventional reality, the person is empty; thus, the eye of Dharma exists regarding the object of merely phenomena. The eye of a Buddha is said to be the knowledge of all objects of knowledge in every aspect; because this is present as a direct perception in the present, the teaching of the five eyes in valid conventional reality expresses the complete purity of what is perceived.In order to express the complete purity of knowledge, the text says, "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth. The mind and mental factors of the three times are the continuum of the mind. Therefore, because the three times are the object, knowing that object is called "knowledge," and it is not called "seeing." Furthermore, one should understand the various natures of the afflicted and the purified, such as "a mind with attachment" and "a mind free from attachment."The expression "as many world systems as that" is an indication, because [the Tathāgata] completely knows the continuum of sentient beings belonging to infinite world systems. In this way, in conventional reality, the Tathāgata possesses the eye of flesh and so forth; therefore, because he accomplishes [the goal] through that, a bodhisattva should abide in aspiration and prayer. This passage demonstrates both types of excellence.The eye of flesh and so forth, when analyzed by the nature of being one or many, are not found; furthermore, it is not reasonable to grasp them by knowing another object. If it were as previously analyzed, one might wonder how the Tathāgata could possess the eye of flesh and so forth, and how he could perfectly know the continuum of the mind. Considering this line of thought, the question "For what reason?" was asked. In order to show how a bodhisattva should accomplish this by entering into meditative equipoise regarding these two—the purity of the bodhisattva and [the nature of the mind]—the text says, "The continuum of the mind, the continuum of the mind," and so forth. The statement "there is no continuum" refers to the ultimate level.Although they are devoid of intrinsic nature, they are spoken of in reliance upon conventional reality; for that very reason, it is said, "the continuum of the mind." The intention is that, otherwise, in ultimate reality, they would not be spoken of, because they transcend the entire scope of verbal expression. The mention of "the continuum of the mind" is an indication, for this is the occasion to state that the eye of flesh and so forth are also taught as being devoid of the nature of an eye; they are taught as being directly perceived. In order to show how the mind should be perfectly grasped in this regard, the question "For what reason?" was asked, and it is connected with the statement "there is no continuum." The mind of the past and so forth is not found, because it is not produced in ultimate reality; however, it is not the case that it is not found because it exists but is impossible to grasp. If that were the case, it would not be taught that there is no continuum of the mind, for the mere fact of not being found does not mean that things are devoid of intrinsic nature. How the mind of the three times does not exist in ultimate reality has been explained previously, and it will also be taught. The mention of "mind" is an indication, and therefore the eye of flesh and so forth, as well as the past and so forth, are also simply not found. With the words "there is no continuum" and so forth, the profound is expressed here. Through the remainder, the vast is expressed.If there is no mind of the three times, then at that time there would also be no mass of merit, for that depends upon the mind.Therefore, having examined how a bodhisattva should strive in order to accomplish the perfection of possessing the mass of merit of the Tathāgata, and having focused on the perfection of possessing the mass of merit, he spoke the words beginning with, "Subhūti, what do you think?"By this, he teaches that if even a son or daughter of a noble family who gives away external objects, such as precious substances, comes to possess a great mass of merit, then why would the Tathāgata, who has practiced difficult deeds for countless, immeasurable eons and has cultivated them for many hundreds of ways, not possess the mass of merit? Therefore, although in the ultimate sense there is no mass of merit, because it exists in the conventional sense, he teaches that a bodhisattva should abide with aspiration and prayer in order to accomplish mastery over it; this also expresses its vastness.Having examined why the mass of merit is not established as existing in the ultimate sense, and in order to show both how a bodhisattva should accomplish this and how the mind should be well-grasped, he spoke the words beginning with, "Subhūti, if..." The word "if" is a synonym for "supposing."The words "the Tathāgata does not speak" mean that he does not engage in verbal expression in the ultimate sense, for he intends that it will become known as such even without being taught. How the mass of merit does not exist in the ultimate sense has already been taught previously. By this, he teaches both that a bodhisattva who has entered into the path to accomplish the perfection of possessing the mass of merit of the Tathāgata should accomplish it by entering into meditative equipoise in which that is not perceived in the ultimate sense, and that the mind should be well-grasped by abandoning attachment to perceiving that in the ultimate sense; this also expresses its profundity.If the mass of merit were non-existent, then the two types of perfect bodies of the Tathāgatas—the perfect body of excellent secondary signs and the perfect body of major marks—which are held to be born from unsurpassable merit, would also become non-existent because they would lack a cause.Therefore, in order to fully accomplish the two types of perfect bodies of the Tathāgata, and for the sake of the bodhisattva who thinks about how to exert effort toward that, he spoke the words beginning with, "Subhūti, what do you think?" with the intention of focusing on the perfect form body of the Tathāgatas. The "form body" should be understood as the body of excellent secondary signs.The body of major marks will be explained below, in the manner of the "ox and the bull." Regarding this, the intention of the noble Subhūti is as follows: just as the mass of merit is, in the ultimate sense, devoid of any inherent mass, so too is the form body unborn. Therefore, one should not view the Tathāgata as being the form body in the ultimate sense. In the conventional sense, however, the form body exists just like a Buddha emanated by magic, and therefore it is appropriate for it to arise from the mass of merit. Thus, it is taught that a bodhisattva should abide with aspiration and prayer in order to accomplish that [form body] through such devotion to the form of a Buddha emanated by magic. There is no repetition of words here, for while at the stage of conduct through devotion one is at the time of aspiring to attain the form body and at the time of making offerings and service to the Tathāgata, one has abandoned such grasping; now, at the stage of the pure superior intention, this is taught in order to dispel the evil conceptualization of those in the retinue who claim that a bodhisattva who has entered the path to accomplish the perfect form body of the Tathāgata has grasping toward form.Thinking, "How then is the form body of the Tathāgatas taught?" one asks, "For what reason?" and connects this with the statement, "One should not view the Tathāgata as being the form body, because it is perfected." This means it is not established; it is not established as the nature of a form body possessing limbs, nor as the nature of an accumulation of atoms, just as previously analyzed. By this, it is shown how a bodhisattva should accomplish it. The phrase "therefore" means that it exists conventionally. It is not that it is non-existent in every way, like the horns of a rabbit. By this, having refuted the extreme of nihilism, it is shown how the mind should be firmly grasped. By all these points, the profound is taught. By teaching that bodhisattvas should exert themselves to accomplish the perfect form body of the Tathāgata conventionally, the vast is also taught. Having taken the perfect body of major marks as the subject, [the sūtra] states, "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth; all the explanations here are the same as the preceding ones.If one should not view the Tathāgata as being the perfected form body, then at that time, the teachings of the Bhagavān would also become non-existent, because they are included within the form body.Therefore, thinking, "How should a bodhisattva exert themselves to accomplish the perfect speech of the Tathāgata?" and for that purpose, having taken the perfect speech as the subject, [the sūtra] states, "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth.In the ultimate sense, because there is no speaker, no object to be spoken of, and no speech, the Tathāgata does not think, "I have taught the Dharma." If it were not so, it would be a misconception, and therefore he would not be omniscient. As for the speaker—the self and so forth—the object to be spoken of—external and internal phenomena—and the speech—the act, whether in the nature of form or sound—that they do not exist has already been explained in detail, because it was previously established that all phenomena are pervaded by emptiness. In the conventional sense, the speaker, the object to be spoken of, and the speech are merely designations for the sake of convenience, which are acceptable when not analyzed, but they do not exist in the ultimate sense. If, even though the suchness of phenomena has been taught in this way, some are confused and think that the three exist in the ultimate sense, then what would happen? Thinking this, [the sūtra] states, "Subhūti, who..." and so forth. Denigration is because it speaks of what is non-existent. Regarding the thought of how one who is non-existent can speak, it states, "by grasping at what is false," meaning that because one is attached to a misconception, one grasps falsely, and thus it is said that it does not exist. By this, it is taught how a bodhisattva should abide, namely, that a bodhisattva who engages in the perfect speech of the Tathāgata should engage by knowing it to be like an echo and so forth.If those three things, such as the explanation, did not exist, how could this diverse nature of words and speech, by which the Bhagavan taught the Dharma—teaching the selflessness of persons and phenomena—be renowned? If they do exist, then that which is to be taught by them, the explanation to be given, and the speaker who teaches them must also exist; thus, thinking that all three must exist by implication, the question "Why is that?" was asked, and here the answer is given as "the teaching of the Dharma." He thinks as follows: If the teaching of the Dharma existed ultimately, would it be an entity of its own characteristic or an entity of a general characteristic? The first alternative is not the case, because all ultimate own-characteristics have been clarified extensively before. The second is also not the case, because if there were no own-characteristic, there would be no basis, and thus nothing at all. If one accepts a general characteristic as a real entity, it is included solely within the own-characteristic, and since that is clarified, the former is also clarified. If one thinks that a general characteristic is an imputed entity by excluding others, then the teaching of the Dharma would be meaningless, and one would be proving what is already established. Even if one were to allow that an own-characteristic exists ultimately, it would not be reasonable for it to teach the Dharma, because the imputation of words by others upon an imputed entity, such as a clear sound, is contradictory in terms of performing a function through sequence or non-sequence; being devoid of all efficacy, it has no connection to consciousness or anything else, and how could it become words while doing nothing at all? Even the impermanence of an own-characteristic is not reasonable as words, because when it is conventionally designated, it is seen, but when it is conventionally established, there is no continuity. It is not reasonable that the conventional designation and the conventional establishment are different, for that would lead to an absurd consequence.Therefore, because there is no subsequent progression, it is not reasonable to express even its own intrinsic nature. If one were to claim that a general entity is also something to be expressed, then because it has become the essence of what is to be expressed, it is the essence of its own intrinsic nature, and thus there is no progression to another object. It is also not reasonable for a single entity to pervade many distinct particulars that are separated by place, time, and so forth. For if the entire self were to be complete in one particular, then at that time, there would be no other nature connected to other particulars that could be understood by whatever nature of that one entity was fully imagined; for the single entity would be lost. If it were to pervade by a single part, it would result in the fault of being composed of parts and not being fully grasped. Thus, if one holds that as many distinct particulars as there are, they are established as being pervaded by a single part of it, then grasping one particular would be grasping a single part, and one might wonder if it is appropriate to grasp it in that way. However, since there is no simultaneous grasping of distinct particulars—which are separated by age, place, time, and so forth—by grasping them from a single particular, it results in there being no conceptualization. Therefore, the expressed and the expression are reasonable only as the essence of a superimposed form, not as they are in reality. For that very reason, the Tathāgata has stated elsewhere: "Whatever names are used to express whatever phenomena, those names do not exist in them; that is the suchness of phenomena." Furthermore, the explanation is also false; thus, the teaching to be explained and the indication that there is an explainer also come from that same door, and are therefore merely particulars. The Tathāgata did not teach them separately as if they were devoid of both. By this, it is shown how a Bodhisattva should practice and how the mind should be well-grasped. By all of this, the profound is shown.The perfection of the mind consists of seven distinct aspects: the foundations of mindfulness, the attainment of perfect awakening, the designation of the great meaning of the Dharma, the designation of the great meaning of the instructions, the complete apprehension of the dharmakāya, the non-abiding in either nirvāṇa or saṃsāra, and the complete purity of dwelling.In this regard, the assembly now lacks conviction, thinking, "In the future, when this profound Dharma is obscured by the thicket of wrong views, how could it possibly be fruitful?" In order to dispel the lack of conviction of those who think in this way, the noble Subhūti, taking as his basis the foundation of mindfulness from among the perfections of the mind, addressed the Blessed One, beginning with the words, "Blessed One..."Did the Blessed One not previously state, "In the future, there will be those who possess ethical conduct and possess qualities," and so forth? Now, in order to show that one should not become attached to the notion that these exist as a unity, nor that they do not exist, he did not say "they exist," but in order to negate the two extremes, he spoke the words, "Subhūti, those..." and so forth. Because in the ultimate sense, the essence of the aggregates, the person, and so on, is not observed, they are not sentient beings; by this, the extreme of reification is negated. Because they exist in a conventional sense as objects of pleasant experience, they are not non-existent; by this, the extreme of nihilism is negated. By teaching that "they will arise," he shows what the unerring foundation of mindfulness of the Blessed One is like for sentient beings, and he teaches that a bodhisattva should dwell in that perfect foundation of mindfulness of the Blessed One through aspiration and prayer. The phrase "they are not sentient beings" indicates the meditative absorption of yoga. If they were not sentient beings, then, having reflected on how the Blessed One could have said, "In the future, there will be those who possess ethical conduct and possess qualities," and so forth, he asked, "For what reason?"The statement "because they are taught to be without sentient beings" means that in the ultimate sense, there is no such thing as a sentient being.They are spoken of in reliance upon the existence of the essence of the aggregates that are established conventionally; therefore, they are called "sentient beings" because they exist conventionally. If it were not so, and they did not exist even conventionally, there would be no speech about them. By this, the mind being well-grasped is shown. By all of this, the profound is expressed. By the Blessed One showing that the foundation of mindfulness is unobstructed toward all sentient beings, the vast is shown.If the Blessed One had not taught any dharma whatsoever, then he would not have attained complete and perfect buddhahood; therefore, the efforts of the bodhisattvas to establish the Tathāgata’s complete and perfect enlightenment would be in vain.For the sake of those who think, "If one desires to attain complete and perfect buddhahood, then at that time there must also be a teaching," he spoke with the intention of complete and perfect enlightenment, saying, "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth. The noble Subhūti, grasping the previous intention, replied, "That is not so." He thinks this because he believes the Blessed One has negated the teaching by intending the ultimate sense. As was previously shown, because in the ultimate sense there is no dharma taught, there is also no complete and perfect buddhahood. Conventionally, however, the Blessed One’s teaching of dharma, the perfect enlightenment, and the path that is its cause do indeed exist. Therefore, a bodhisattva should strive to establish the essence of the unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment in its true conventional sense; by this, it is shown how a bodhisattva should abide. Previously, at the time of seeking the instructions, the conceptualization of the bodhisattva who thinks that complete and perfect enlightenment is in the ultimate sense was dispelled; now, at the time of seeking the buddha-ground, because such conceptualization of others is dispelled, there is no fault of repeating the words. Regarding the thought of what that unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment, which the Blessed One has established in the true conventional sense, is like, he spoke, "Even a little," and so forth.When the gnosis resides in that, the essence of realizing the selflessness of phenomena in its entirety—without even the slightest apprehension of the nature of phenomena that grasp at their own characteristics—is what the Tathāgata calls unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment. It is "unsurpassed" because it is superior to the gnosis of outsiders, learners, and those beyond learning. It is called "perfect, complete enlightenment" because it is the essence of having realized the suchness of all entities exactly as it is; this is the intended meaning. Regarding that, it is said that they are "non-existent" as a logical reason for the non-apprehension of phenomena. Because they are non-existent, they are not apprehended; it is not that they exist and yet are not apprehended, for if all phenomena existed, they would become objects of the apprehension of the Tathāgata’s gnosis. By this, the essence of realizing the selflessness of phenomena has been taught. Now, in order to teach the essence of realizing the selflessness of persons, it is said, "Again, Subhūti," and so forth."That phenomenon is equal," means that in all phenomena realized by him, there is an equality in the selflessness of persons."There is nothing whatsoever that is unequal," means that in every respect it is unerring, because the mental continuum that grasps at a self has abandoned the attachment to entities as real. The Tathāgata has abandoned the grasping at a self along with its latent tendencies; therefore, the essence of realizing the selflessness of persons—which is that very thing—is called unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment, and it is not that of others. Regarding the question of by what means that phenomenon is equal, it is said, "There are no sentient beings," and so forth. By all of this, the way in which one should accomplish this through meditative equipoise is taught.Regarding the question of how one manifests complete awakening, it is said, "By all wholesome phenomena," and so forth; the intended meaning is that one manifests complete awakening through wholesome phenomena that are the essence of the accumulations of merit and gnosis.If, because they are non-existent, not even the slightest phenomenon can be apprehended, how can it be that "wholesome phenomena" exist? Regarding the question of why one manifests complete awakening through them, it is said, "wholesome phenomena," and so forth; in the ultimate sense, phenomena are indeed non-existent.Because they exist conventionally, it is said "wholesome phenomena," and therefore there is no fault in saying that one manifests complete awakening through wholesome phenomena. By this, it is shown that the mind is well-held, as it dispels the distraction of grasping at the extremes of superimposition and deprecation. By all of this, profundity is taught. By fully expressing the very nature of perfect, complete enlightenment—which is the realization of the selflessness of persons and phenomena without remainder—vastness is also taught.Reflecting on how one should understand the perfect, complete awakening of the Tathāgata, and having examined it, the Blessed One spoke the words "Again, Subhūti," and so forth, in order to demonstrate its existence by designating it as a phenomenon of great significance.The "King of Mountains, Mount Meru" is an illustration; even the merit gained by filling infinite world systems with precious substances is incomparable. The phrase "from this prajñāpāramitā" indicates all the phenomena of the Mahāyāna, as it does not express mere signs. The word "between" serves to include those [phrases] such as "the thousand-fold," "the hundred-thousand-fold," and "the analogies and causes." Thus, because of the reason of designating it as a phenomenon of great significance, one knows the Tathāgata’s perfect, complete enlightenment—which is the nature of his perfected mind—to be unexcelled, for without such a perfect enlightenment, it would be impossible to teach a phenomenon such as this. Therefore, one should abide in order to accomplish through aspiration and prayer such a perfected mind; by all of this, it is shown how a bodhisattva should abide, and by this very fact, vastness is also expressed. That perfect enlightenment should be viewed as having the nature of a true conventional reality, not an ultimate reality, for the reasons explained previously. Although not explicitly stated, it is implicitly shown that one enters into meditative equipoise, that the mind is well-held, and that there is also the [cessation of] defilement.When the Bhagavan abides in supramundane wisdom, it is not surprising that, due to being in a state of profound meditative equipoise, the perception of sentient beings and so forth does not arise. In order to show that even when he abides in mundane wisdom—at times when he is not in meditative equipoise—while bestowing the prophecy of liberation upon sentient beings, the perception of sentient beings and so forth also does not arise, and to indicate that this is the cause for establishing the instruction as having great meaning, thereby revealing that the Bhagavan’s perfect, unsurpassed mind is known, he spoke the words "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth, with the intention of teaching an instruction of great meaning.Having asked, he did not wait for an answer, but as if possessing a sense of urgency, he spoke the words "Subhūti, it should not be viewed in that way," and so forth. Therefore, this shows that a Bodhisattva should abide with aspiration and prayer regarding such a cause for the Bhagavan’s perfect instruction of great meaning.If sentient beings were truly existent, they would become a cause for defilement; does the Tathāgata not think in this way? Or, having examined the thought of one who thinks, "Is it because there are no sentient beings?" he asked, "For what reason?" And, in order to show that because sentient beings, which are of the nature of the aggregates and the person, do not exist in the ultimate sense, they are not perceived in that way, he spoke the words, "Because there is no sentient being that the Tathāgata has liberated." By this, he has shown what is to be accomplished by the Bodhisattva through entering into such a meditative equipoise. Regarding the thought, "How is it known that they do not exist?" he spoke the words, "Subhūti, if..." and so forth. The intention here is this: the Tathāgata’s wisdom engages with knowable objects just as they are. If it were not so, how could he be the Tathāgata, having not abandoned the obscurations? Therefore, if sentient beings existed, then at that time the Tathāgata would perceive them clearly, for because he perceives the self directly, he is free from doubt. That very thing would become a firm grasping at a self of those beings. Therefore, because the binding of the entire net of defilements, which arises from the cause of grasping at a self, would be light or manifest, if at that time he had not abandoned the very firm obscuration of the binding of attachment and so forth, the Bhagavan would not have attained the rank of Tathāgata; yet, because the Bhagavan has attained that rank, it follows that he has abandoned all obscurations. By abandoning the obscurations, the entire mountain of grasping at a self is demolished. Therefore, it is not that he does not know that sentient beings do not exist.Even though it is devoid of a self, there is a grasping at a self; does the defining characteristic of the view of a self not exist? Regarding the question, "Bhagavān, how should one not conceive of a self and so forth?" the passage beginning with "Subhūti, what is called 'grasping at a self'..." was spoken. If one were to grasp at any entity such as a self, then at that time, Bhagavān, a grasping at a self would arise for one who has abandoned the obscurations; however, because there is nothing whatsoever to be grasped as a self, the Tathāgata has taught that there is no grasping. Regarding the question, "Then what is meant by 'grasping at a self'?" the passage beginning with "That also..." was spoken. "Foolish beings" are those who, lacking learning and so forth, do not clearly understand what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted. "Ordinary beings" are those who are distinct from the Āryas because they lack discernment. Since some ordinary beings, having listened to the authentic treatises and abiding in appropriate mental engagement, have faith in the selflessness of phenomena, they do not grasp at a self because they are firmly convinced of the truth; thus, "foolish beings" is stated in order to exclude them. If only "foolish beings" were mentioned, then since such ordinary beings who are learned in the aggregates and so forth have not yet generated the path of the Āryas, they are "foolish selves"; therefore, in order to indicate the distinction of foolish beings, [it is said that] even though that is a mistaken grasping at a self, because they have become foolish, it appears to them as if there is a grasping at a self. Therefore, due to the power of their conceptualization, it is taught in that way as "grasping at a self."That would not merely fail to be true, but would result in an absurdity; for why, by the application of terms such as "selfless," would one not also apprehend the self and the like as true? If there is no self, one might wonder, "To whom do the 'ordinary beings' refer?" In response to this, it is stated, "the childish ordinary beings," and so forth. In the ultimate sense, there are no beings; it is spoken in reliance upon the conventional, and thus there is no fault. By all of this, the elimination of the extremes of superimposition and denial is shown, thereby demonstrating how the mind is thoroughly grasped. By all of this, the profundity is directly expressed; and the teaching that the entire realm of sentient beings is the cause for establishing the great meaning of the instructions also demonstrates the vastness of the perfect mind.If there were no childish ordinary beings, how could there be a Tathāgata possessing a perfect body adorned with the excellent marks and secondary signs? Thinking that ordinary beings, having generated the bodhicitta arising from the root of compassion and engaging in the perfections, become the perfect Tathāgata adorned with marks and the like, and that if those beings did not exist, there would be no root, and thus how could there be such a perfect Tathāgata—those in the assembly who have accumulated no small amount of realization, yet who are attached to forms and the like as real entities, think in this way. For their sake, focusing on the apprehension of the dharmakāya, the words "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth were spoken. Previously, the dharmakāya had not been established, but because this was spoken in order to establish the dharmakāya, there is no fault of verbal repetition. Realizing that the perfect marks, when examined in the ultimate sense, are not established as the essence of a composite entity or as an accumulation of atoms, and holding to the previous intention, the noble Subhūti replied, "It is not so." The Blessed One, in this very place, spoke of another justification, saying, "Subhūti, if..." and so forth.If the Tathāgata were distinguished merely by the possession of perfect marks, then, because the reason for such a designation would be the same, why would a wheel-turning monarch not also be a Tathāgata? If one were to argue that the Blessed One’s perfect marks are distinct because they reside in a domain, are clear, and are complete, whereas those of a wheel-turning monarch are not, and therefore the latter is not called a Tathāgata, that too is unreasonable; for the distinctions of residing in a domain and so forth do not differ in any way from the nature of material things. Therefore, if the Tathāgata were distinguished by phenomena such as marks that are of the nature of material things, then a wheel-turning monarch would also be a Tathāgata, which is not the case. Thus, it is intended that the Tathāgata is distinguished solely by his realization of the nature of all phenomena exactly as they are. By this, it is shown that a bodhisattva should abide with aspiration and prayer in such a body, which has the Tathāgata’s wisdom as its cause. Now, in order to show that one should not be attached even to that wisdom of the Tathāgata in the ultimate sense, the dharmakāya is established, and the manner in which a bodhisattva should practice by entering into meditative equipoise is taught through two verses.In that regard, the preceding verse teaches how one should not view the Tathāgata, and by whom he is not seen.How should one not view him? By way of the conventional designations of seeing and so forth. Who are those by whom he is not seen? Those who have entered into the path of wrong abandonment. By the phrase "viewing him as form," this indicates the conventional designation of viewing a person who is attached to form as having the form of a person or a phenomenon, adorned in the ultimate sense with marks and so forth. The phrase "knowing him by sound" means that I know the Tathāgata in such a way, thinking, "He is like this, he is of this nature," based on sound. This indicates the conventional designation of hearing. These two conventional designations are illustrative; they also encompass differentiating and cognizing. Those beings who have entered into the path of wrong abandonment do not see me correctly because they have entered into a wrong path. Because this abandons, it is called "abandonment," which refers to the path. That is "wrong" because it has become perverted; that, too, is a cause for not seeing. If one wonders, "Then how should the Buddha be viewed?" the text states, "viewing him as the dharmatā," and so forth. The true nature of phenomena is what is called the dharmatā; because it is established by reasoning and scripture, it is the essence of what has been peaceful from the beginning. That very thing is expressed by synonyms such as "suchness," "dharmadhātu," "ultimate reality," "signlessness," and "the absolute."Because it exists in that way at all times, it is *tathatā* (suchness). Since all the qualities of a Buddha arise by taking that as their object, and because it serves as their cause, it is *dharmadhātu* (the expanse of phenomena). Because it is not erroneous, it is *yathārtha* (the real), and because it is the culmination of that, it is *bhūtakoṭi* (the ultimate limit). Because all marks of entities, such as blue and so forth, are absent in it, it is *animitta* (signless). Because it is the object of the supreme wisdom, it is *paramārtha* (the ultimate).Thinking, "For what reason should it be viewed as *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena)?" the text states "Dharmakāya." The term "kāya" (body) refers to the nature. Therefore, the meaning here is as follows: those who are established as a Tathāgata, having the cause of perfect wisdom, are in the ultimate sense the nature of the *dharma*. One should view those things as being of the essence of that which they are the nature of; one should not view one thing as having the essence of another. If that were the case, then *dharmatā* would become the nature of appearances.If that is not the case, then thinking, "How can one be capable of seeing those things indicated by it?" the text states "Dharmatā" and so forth. Is it that one does not see because one is incapable? Or is it that if one were to fully understand it, it would involve a fault? Thinking this, the text states "incapable" and so forth. If the nature of a *dharmin* (a phenomenon possessing properties) were established, then one might be capable of cognizing its *dharmatā*. However, at the time when, in the ultimate sense, there is no *dharmin* established as having its own essence, how could one be capable of cognizing that *dharmatā* as a separate continuum? The intention is that it does not exist as something separate.If that is the case, then if the essence of perfect wisdom—the *dharmin*—and the Buddhas themselves are not established in the ultimate sense and thus are not seen, how then should one view it as *dharmatā*? There is no fault in that, for it is precisely by not seeing all *dharmins* in the ultimate sense that one sees *dharmatā*. Since *dharmatā* is of the essence of non-arising, how could it be grasped by grasping at arising, which is incompatible with it? Grasping at a vase does not constitute grasping at its non-arising. By this, it teaches that one should not view the Tathāgata as a *rūpakāya* (form body), but should view him as a *dharmakāya*.Even though the Tathāgata is not of the nature of possessing perfect physical marks, it is reasonable that the defining characteristic of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment arises from the causes of perfect physical marks. In order to dispel the doubt that a bodhisattva, having been seen by physiognomists as possessing perfect physical marks, was therefore prophesied by the Bhagavan to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, he spoke [the words] beginning with, "Subhūti, what do you think?" The intention is that if perfect physical marks were the cause of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, then at that time a cakravartin would also become [a Buddha]. There is no fault in saying that the cause of the prophecy is not that physiognomists saw such signs. By this, the supreme cultivation of the mind is taught. By all of this, profundity is taught. By teaching the defining characteristic of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, which has realized the nature of all phenomena without exception in conventional reality, vastness is also taught.If, because all phenomena are non-existent in the ultimate sense, that reality cannot be cognized, then in that case you would become a proponent of nihilism.Because of the doubt that the Tathāgata also does not exist, and therefore a non-abiding nirvāṇa is not established, he spoke [the words] beginning with, "Subhūti, what do you think, those who have truly entered the bodhisattva vehicle," in order to focus on not abiding in saṃsāra and nirvāṇa. There is no analysis that destroys what has occurred, because one realizes the nature of phenomena just as it abides. Therefore, it is said:"In this, there is nothing to be removed,And nothing to be established.Truly seeing the truth itself,One who sees truly is liberated."There is no analysis of nihilism that obstructs the arising of future phenomena, because the nature of phenomena is taught just as it abides. Since it is accepted that all phenomena, when not analyzed, arise according to conditions as they are, the Buddha Bhagavan, by the power of great compassion, possesses emanations and so forth in the nature of true conventional reality; and because it is accepted that he does not cut the stream of entering saṃsāra by teaching methods just as they are for the sake of those to be trained, by this, the Bhagavan’s non-abiding in nirvāṇa is taught, and the necessity of abiding in such a body of the Bhagavan through aspiration and prayer is also taught. Because it is considered that if it were accepted that the Bhagavan enters saṃsāra in that way, he would become saṃsāra itself, he spoke [the words] beginning with, "Again, Subhūti," in order to teach the state of not abiding in saṃsāra."Selflessness" means that, like an illusion, it is dependent upon others. It is not the nature of a self by itself, for if it were permanent, it would be contradictory as a cause due to [the issues of] sequence and non-sequence; and if it were not a cause, it would do nothing, and thus it would be impossible for it to be a bestower of blessings. There is also no self that has been blessed by another. Therefore, in both ways, all phenomena are selfless. As it is said: "O monks, childish beings who lack learning designate and engage in 'self' and 'mine,' but in this [reality], there is no 'self' or 'mine'." By this, the patience regarding the selflessness of the person is shown for all phenomena. By the phrase "non-arising," the patience regarding the selflessness of phenomena is shown. If entities were to arise, would they arise from having no cause or from having a cause? If one speculates that they arise from having a cause, would they arise from a permanent cause or an impermanent cause? Regarding that, since entities appear occasionally, the first speculation is not tenable, for if they were independent, there would be no distinction in any respect, and they would be permanently existent or non-existent, just like the time of existence and non-existence. Therefore, because they arise occasionally, the second position is also not tenable, for if the power of permanent things cannot be differentiated by other auxiliary conditions, and if they are dependent on nothing, then why would they produce results sequentially rather than simultaneously? It is not reasonable that a result whose causes are complete would not appear occasionally; why then would it arise sequentially? Those who assert that there is an intrinsic nature as the cause of entities are also, in reality, admitting that there is no existence, for if an intrinsic nature were established, it would be a cause, but if it is not established, it is not, because it is characterized by being devoid of all power.If the intrinsic nature of a phenomenon is established, then one must admit that it is established without a cause; for if one does not accept that there is some other, distinct cause, how could it not be causeless? Since a phenomenon is not other than its intrinsic nature, if it is established, it is established as such, and thus it becomes causeless. If it were not so, then since it would not be established when it is established, how could it be of an intrinsic nature that is non-distinct from that? Therefore, the refutation of the position that asserts causelessness is the same here as well.It is also not appropriate to posit a third position, because it is contradictory for a cause to exist either simultaneously or non-simultaneously with the effect. For if it were to become a cause in this way, one might wonder whether it would be simultaneous with the effect or at a different time. It cannot be simultaneous, because the entity itself, not having attained its own state, is devoid of all capacity and thus has no connection to any effect whatsoever. The entity itself is merely the intrinsic nature of the state of having attained the effect simultaneously with it, according to its own nature; there is no connection of that to the effect.If they are at different times, then it would be separated by another time, and it would become like the Vaibhāṣikas, who accept the cause of maturation as a cause, or it would arise from an offering; or perhaps it would be like the Sautrāntikas, who claim that the destruction and arising of cause and effect are equal, like the rising and falling of the pans of a scale. If the effect arises after being separated by another time, then one would have to admit that it arises from the very state of destruction. Since that is devoid of all capacity, it is not reasonable for destruction to be the entity of a cause.If that is not the case, how could a non-acting entity become something that is destroyed? If one were to offer worship to the entirety of an object, then at that very moment, the worship would become simultaneous; there is no other way for two partless entities to be worshipped in their entirety except by becoming simultaneous. Therefore, just as if atoms were to be cut in their entirety, they would become mere atoms, so too it is difficult to avoid the conclusion that an eon also becomes a mere moment. If one worships with only one part, then it would possess limbs. Therefore, all phenomena are, in the ultimate sense, unborn; they merely appear as if they arise due to the falsity of unexamined delight, similar to the nature of what appears to a deluded consciousness. By what logic can one argue that conventional consensus is not a valid cognition, and that it is therefore unreasonable to deconstruct it because it is accepted by everyone from cowherds upwards as the cause and effect of phenomena? It is because conventional consensus regarding forms and the like is deconstructed by valid cognition. Therefore, the Bhagavan states in the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra*:Having refuted valid cognitions such as the eye,The eye, the ear, and the nose are not valid cognitions.The tongue, the body, and the mind are not valid cognitions.If these faculties were valid,What would there be for the noble path to do?It is stated:"In this way, these faculties are not valid cognitions,For by their very nature they are inert and indeterminate.Therefore, whoever desires the path to nirvāṇa,Let them perform the task of the noble path."Whatever definition of direct perception the masters have provided is also direct perception only conventionally; it should be viewed as a means of entering into the ultimate. Conventionally, one does not dispute or examine; therefore, because it is taught conventionally, it cannot withstand analysis. For this reason, the Bhagavan has refuted the arising of phenomena from self or other in the *Śālistamba-sūtra* and similar texts. As it is said in the *Ārya-laṅkāvatāra*: "Great Sage, because they do not arise from existence or non-existence, all phenomena are unborn." It is stated in the *Mahā-prajñāpāramitā*: "Subhūti, that which is not even slightly born is called 'non-arising'." The wisdom that is present regarding that is called "forbearance for the unborn nature of phenomena." As it is said in the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*:"That which has no intrinsic nature,How could it be conditioned by another?Without intrinsic nature, how could it produce another?This cause has been well taught by the Sugata."Furthermore: "The arising of phenomena is conventional;"In the ultimate sense, there is no intrinsic nature," it is also said. If one were to ask, "Is this said with the intention that all these things are of the nature of the conceptually constructed?" the answer is no, because all intrinsic natures have already been refuted by valid cognition. By this, it is taught that if even others who possess only a small root of virtue do not experience the suffering of cyclic existence, then why would a Bodhisattva, who has attained forbearance for the unborn nature of phenomena, who has given rise to a great accumulation of wisdom, and who has attained the generation of an unsurpassed accumulation of merit, experience the suffering of cyclic existence? In this way, suffering is experienced in cyclic existence in two forms, characterized by physical and mental distress. The former is the result of negative karma, and the latter arises from ignorance, that is, it arises from wrong views. For a Bodhisattva who has attained forbearance for the unborn nature of phenomena, both causes of suffering—negative karma and ignorance—are absent. Without the causes, it is impossible to be touched by the latent tendencies of suffering. By this, it is taught how a Bodhisattva should practice. One might wonder: "Even if one has already generated an extremely vast accumulation of merit, will one not still be in cyclic existence like sentient beings who engage in form and so forth? How is it taught that merely by generating a vast accumulation of merit, one does not abide in cyclic existence?" To address this doubt, the words "Subhūti" and so forth were spoken.By this, even if one has generated a mass of merit, because one clings to it as a perversion, one possesses an grasping of the mass of merit; since the root of all defilement—the perversion—has not been abandoned, even if one attains a superior state of existence, it is classified as being within saṃsāra. A bodhisattva, having attained the patience for the unborn nature of phenomena, has no clinging to the mass of merit as being truly real; therefore, because the root of all defilement—profound ignorance—has been abandoned, it is taught that they do not abide in saṃsāra.In order to dispel the conceptualizations of others, the noble Subhūti expresses a contradiction, asking, "Should one not embrace it just as the Bhagavan has not embraced the intention?" His thought is this: "The Bhagavan has stated in various sūtras that a bodhisattva should embrace the mass of merit, yet here he states that it should not be embraced; how can this not be a contradiction?" The Bhagavan, in order to show the intention by which both were stated, said, "One may indeed embrace it." The statement "embrace it" refers to the method of embracing characterized by accomplishment. Here, however, the characteristic of grasping wrongly is being dispelled, so there is no contradiction. Grasping wrongly is grasping the path wrongly. By this, the mind is shown to be well-embraced through the abandonment of that conceptualization. Furthermore, beginning with "Subhūti, whatever son or daughter of noble family," the vast aspect is taught. The remaining previous sections taught the profound aspect. By all these points, the extremes of permanence and annihilation are blocked, and the Middle Way is expressed. The non-abiding in saṃsāra and nirvāṇa has already been explained.It should be stated that the abiding is completely pure. This is also divided into three types: abiding through deportment, abiding by having mastery over the world of vessels and sentient beings, and abiding by having no defilements whatsoever.In this regard, if one thinks, "If the Buddha is to be viewed as the Dharmakāya and not as the Rūpakāya, then how is it not contradictory to the scriptures that proclaim the Bhagavan’s four modes of deportment, his birth, his departure, and so forth?"—then, for the sake of such a person, focusing on the perfect abiding through deportment, he spoke the words beginning with, "Subhūti, whatever..." The two terms "walking" or "coming" indicate the act of walking. The remaining terms indicate the other modes of deportment, such as standing, in their respective order. The mention of deportment is merely illustrative; therefore, it should be understood that birth and the rest are also indicated here. Those who cling to the literal meaning of the Bhagavan’s deportment and other activities as described in the scriptures are clinging to a perversion, and thus they do not understand the meaning intended by the Tathāgata. The Bhagavan is not a differentiation of the Rūpakāya; he is the purity of primordial wisdom. Because that primordial wisdom lacks a physical body, it is impossible for it to walk or perform other such actions in a conventional sense. Walking and the like are differentiated based on the specific location of the physical aggregates; therefore, those actions are spoken of in reliance upon the Bhagavan’s Nirmāṇakāya, not in reliance upon the Jñānakāya, for in that [Jñānakāya], walking and the like are impossible in both conventional and ultimate terms. Therefore, it is shown that a bodhisattva should abide through aspiration and prayer in such a state of perfect abiding through deportment. If one thinks, "If the Tathāgata does not possess walking and the like, then how is it taught that he is differentiated by 'having gone' (gata) as in the name 'Tathāgata'?"—having examined this thought, he said, "Why is that?" and this is to be connected with the statement, "They do not understand the meaning of what I have explained."In response, the expression "Tathāgata" and so forth is stated. This is said with the following thought: the designation is not distinguished by "going" (gśegs pa), but is distinguished by "realization" (thugs su chud pa), for the term "going" signifies the meaning of realization. Because he has realized and understood the suchness of things exactly as it abides, he is the Tathāgata. Alternatively, just as the Buddhas of the past realized the suchness of things without error, so too has this one known and realized it, and thus he is the Tathāgata. That is also because, in terms of authentic conventional reality, there is no conceptualization regarding others in the nature of the wisdom-body. Furthermore, because there is no physical body, it is impossible for there to be any "going" or the like even in conventional reality. In the ultimate sense, because there is no birth, it is impossible for there to be any "going" at all. Therefore, because he has realized the nature of things as such, he becomes the lord of all the world, and because he is worthy of offerings, he is called an Arhat.Because he has perfectly and completely realized [the truth], he is called a Samyaksambuddha. The thought here is that if it were not so, the form body would be of the nature of an insentient thing, and thus it would not be called by that name. By this, meditative equipoise and the perfect grasping of the mind are indicated. By all of these points, profundity is indicated. Because it is shown that, conventionally, the Tathāgata’s emanated form body relies upon going and so forth without obstruction throughout infinite world realms, vastness is also indicated. Since any emanated form body of the Tathāgata, as well as any mind-made body, is devoid of the nature of being one or many, it is shown to be false, like a Buddha emanated by magic; therefore, having analyzed the world of vessels and sentient beings, and having taken the state of abiding as the basis, the expression "Subhūti" and so forth is stated. Previously, it was shown that the bodhisattva on the stage of engaging through aspiration analyzes these, but now, by showing the abiding of the Bhagavan on the stage of a Buddha, there is no repetition of words. Here too, by realizing that [the Tathāgata] is devoid of the nature of being one or many through two types of methods, selflessness is taught.The statement, "For example, if it were reduced to a mass of infinitesimal particles," indicates the method for thinning out [the concept of form] by realizing that it is devoid of the nature of being a single entity; the explanation here is also as before.Are infinitesimal particles not non-existent because they have distinct directional parts? Thinking, "How can they become an aggregation?" [the questioner] asks, "For that reason," and in response, the Bhagavan states, "If..." The thought here is this: the aggregation that is analyzed into infinitesimal particles merely as a method to reverse the grasping at a single entity is not something that the Bhagavan has stated to exist in the ultimate sense. If it were not so, since the aggregation of infinitesimal particles is famously evident to everyone, the Bhagavan would not have taught "an aggregation of infinitesimal particles," for it would be famous even without his teaching it. By this, it is shown that one should abide through aspiration and longing in such a state of abiding where the Tathāgata’s form is analyzed.Thinking that if there were no aggregation, why would the Bhagavan have stated, "Are those aggregations of infinitesimal particles numerous?" [Subhūti] asks, "For what reason?" The statement, "Because they are not aggregations," means that since those infinitesimal particles, which exist by being differentiated into directions such as east and north, are not established by their own nature, it is not logically sound for them to be an aggregation in the ultimate sense.It is merely stated to dispel the grasping at a single entity; therefore, it is called an "aggregation of infinitesimal particles." If there were no distinct directional parts, then infinitesimal particles would not be surrounded by other infinitesimal particles from the far side, the near side, above, below, and from distinct directional parts. Therefore, they would not become extensive, just as is the case with consciousness and mental factors. It is not logically sound to say that the parts themselves become infinitesimal particles, for the same analysis applies there as well. If you argue that even if they were to become so, they would have no contact, that is not acceptable; for if infinitesimal particles were to become partless in nature, what would you have established? A partless nature cannot be established as a real entity; therefore, our own position is established. We do not assert that particles are of the nature of many forms in an arbitrary way, so if infinitesimal particles have no contact, what is it that you claim is established? Since you admit that the infinitesimal particles you posit as partless entities reside in distinct directions such as east and north, you have admitted that they have directional parts; therefore, it follows that they possess limbs. Thus, because the consequence is proven, the basis of your logical reason is not established. It is also not the case that they are not fixed as one, like consciousness and mental factors, because they lack physical form and therefore do not reside in directions; they do not reside in directions such as east and north. Therefore, it is taught: "It is not the eye, nor is it form; it does not reside between those two. Where it resides, it is neither existent nor non-existent." The consequence is sufficient. By this, it is shown that having understood the absence of a nature of many, one should engage in the meditative equipoise of yoga and the firm grasping of the mind, which are the methods for making appearances non-existent. The statement, "Are those aggregations of infinitesimal particles numerous?" indicates vastness, while the remainder indicates profundity.Now, focusing on the fact that the Tathāgata dwells by having deconstructed the world of sentient beings, the passage beginning with "the world system of the great trichiliocosm" was spoken. Since the world of the receptacle has already been explained, here the "world system" is understood as the world of sentient beings. The mention of "great trichiliocosm" in both cases signifies that the world systems are limitless. Therefore, the statement "the Tathāgata has spoken of them as not being world systems" means that the world of sentient beings, which is the nature of the five aggregates, is also devoid of the nature of being one or many, and is thus explained as before. By this, it is shown that a Bodhisattva should abide in such a state—where the Tathāgata dwells by having deconstructed the world of sentient beings—through aspiration and prayer. By making it devoid of appearance, it is also shown how this meditative equipoise is to be accomplished. Now, in order to show how the mind is to be firmly grasped, the question "Why is that?" is asked, and it is to be connected with the statement "the Tathāgata has spoken of them as not being world systems."In response, the Blessed One spoke the passage beginning with "If." If the world of sentient beings were, as it is commonly reputed, to exist ultimately as a coarse, unitary entity, then at that time, the Tathāgata, having realized the reality of entities exactly as they abide, would be grasping it as a whole. Therefore, the cause of grasping at a self is merely the grasping at the nature of the aggregates as a whole; thus, that very thing becomes the Tathāgata’s firm grasping at a whole, and it is intended that this has not been abandoned. That is not the case. Therefore, the grasping at a whole which the Blessed One taught to childish beings as the cause of grasping at a self in another context is, in the ultimate sense, a lack of grasping, because there is no nature of a grasped whole that is either one or many.It is merely taught conventionally as the nature reputed to childish beings, and therefore it is called "grasping at a whole." To establish that meaning, the Blessed One spoke of the "meaning of grasping at a whole."What is being taught? It is taught that the expression "grasping at a whole" is conventionally used, but because it does not exist in the ultimate sense, that phenomenon is inexpressible. If there is no such grasped whole, then at that time there is also no grasping of it; thinking, "How then can it be called 'grasping at a whole' conventionally?" one examines it, and it is taught that "it is grasped by childish, ordinary beings." Childish beings, due to the power of delusion, grasp at what does not exist as if it did exist; thus, the convention is applied based on their way of thinking, and it is intended that there is no contradiction. Therefore, they are called "childish beings"; if it were not so, how could they be childish beings, given that they apply conventions according to how things actually are? Here, how the mind is to be firmly grasped has already been taught. The extensive and the profound should also be applied here as before. By this, it is taught that when all phenomena are, in the ultimate sense, empty of intrinsic nature, how could the Tathāgata’s form body and wisdom body be considered to have an ultimate nature, since at the root there are no sentient beings? Now, the passage beginning with "Subhūti, if some..." teaches the method by which one should be equanimous in all situations, having entered into the yogic meditative equipoise. The connection is to be applied as follows: if there is no grasping at a whole, then at that time there is no view of the transitory collection, which arises from the root; therefore, wondering how the Blessed One taught the view of the transitory collection among the five views, for that purpose, the passage beginning with "Subhūti, if some..." was spoken. By teaching here how to be non-conceptual, who is non-conceptual, what is to be non-conceptualized, by what one is non-conceptual, and what non-conceptualization is, the method of entering into yogic meditative equipoise is correctly taught. Regarding that, from "Subhūti, if some..." up to "therefore it is called 'view of a self'," this teaches how to be non-conceptual. How so? Other non-Buddhist schools explain a self, but the Blessed One, establishing that there is no self in the person, taught the "view of a self" in order to refute the self.By thoroughly dismantling the view of a self, one establishes the selflessness of phenomena; this is what is meant by the inquiry, "How did the Tathāgata speak of that which is not a view?" If one does not grasp that view of a self as being truly existent, then by engaging in this way, the bodhisattva enters into meditative equipoise; because there is no conceptualization, that is the method for entering into it.Subhūti, the phrase "has truly entered the bodhisattva vehicle" fully demonstrates who it is that engages in non-conceptuality. The phrase "all phenomena" indicates that toward which one is to be non-conceptual. The phrases "should be known, should be seen, should be resolved upon" express by what means one is to be non-conceptual. By what means is one to be non-conceptual? By knowledge, by vision, and by resolution. Regarding these, knowledge is the wisdom arising from hearing. Vision is the wisdom arising from reflection, for it is that which brings about realization. Resolution is the wisdom arising from meditation; here, the term "resolution" is intended to express a superior aspiration. That is accomplished through the power of meditation; therefore, the wisdom arising from meditation is spoken of as "resolution" when in the stage of the factors concordant with certainty.The phrase "one should resolve in such a way that one does not even abide in the notion of phenomena" demonstrates what that non-conceptuality is.The statement "the Tathāgata has spoken of that as being without perception" is presented here as a logical reason. Because that which is to be perceived is itself empty of the nature of being one or many, in the ultimate sense, it is without perception. The Tathāgata spoke of it in another way by relying upon the conventional. The intention is that if one knows it to be false and abides in that, how could one become conceptually attached? The method for entering into meditative equipoise in all situations has been explained. The absence of defilement is also of two types: the absence of defilement in teaching and the absence of defilement in cyclic existence.In this regard, if there is no perception of phenomena, then when the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma to sentient beings, if that perception arises, how could there be no thorough affliction? Thinking, "If one abides until the end of cyclic existence for the sake of sentient beings out of compassion, how could one not be thoroughly afflicted by the perception of phenomena?" and having examined this, the Tathāgata, through that very perfection of his mind, teaches that there is no thorough affliction in teaching, and through the verse, he shows that there is no thorough affliction in cyclic existence; for this reason, he says "Subhūti" and so forth. Previously, in other contexts, the praises of world-systems were taught to express merit, but now, in the context of there being no thorough affliction, he does not state the merit when teaching the infinite world-systems, so that the words do not become repetitive. Here too, the reasoning should be stated as before. "Having taken up" means having recited it by heart. "Grasping" refers to the words. "Reading" refers to reading from a book or the like. "Comprehending" is a synonym for grasping the meaning. By this, he fully demonstrates that because this Dharma is of great significance, a Bodhisattva must inevitably abide with aspiration and prayer in such a great and significant teaching of the Dharma.Although it has been explained, in order to show how it is explained that there is no thorough affliction, he says, "How does he correctly and thoroughly teach?" and so forth. The intention is this: although it is taught that all phenomena are, in the ultimate sense, unborn and inexpressible, those phenomena are not explained as having the nature of being inexpressible. This is taught in the following way: he teaches in such a way that the person being trained thinks, "All phenomena are unborn from the very beginning and are therefore inexpressible; hence, they are not things to be taught by anyone." In this way, he teaches without being afflicted, because it is for the sake of the non-erroneous meaning. If it were not so, he would be teaching erroneously and thus would be afflicted. Therefore, when the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma, although he enters into pure worldly wisdom and perceptions of phenomena as such arise, because he has no grasping at them as being truly real, he does not incur the fault of being afflicted. By this, he demonstrates meditative equipoise, the thorough holding of the mind, and profundity. By the former, he demonstrated vastness.Now, he sets forth the entire body of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and by means of a verse, he demonstrates that there is no thorough affliction of *saṃsāra*. This verse fully demonstrates four types of characteristics of the conditioned: the characteristic of nature, the characteristic of the object of experience, the characteristic of realizing the drawbacks, and the characteristic of realizing the definitive emergence. Regarding that, the nature of the five *skandha*s, which are entities as they appear, are dependent and interconnected; because they are produced by the gathering of causes and conditions, they are called "conditioned." The nature of all of these should be viewed like the stars. Just as stars appear at night but do not appear during the day, conditioned phenomena appear when there is the darkness of the fault of ignorance, but they do not appear when the light of the sun of wisdom arises; therefore, they should be viewed as having the nature of stars. Conditioned phenomena that have the nature of grasping at persons and phenomena should be viewed like a cataract, because they are the cause of the appearance of what is non-existent. The characteristic of consciousness should be viewed like a butter lamp, because it burns in dependence upon the wick of karma and the oil of craving. In this way, by means of these analogies, he fully demonstrates the characteristic of the nature of the conditioned.The analogy of an illusion fully demonstrates the characteristic of the object of experience, because it appears in a deceptive manner. Regarding that, the two types of characteristics of realizing the drawbacks are the nature of the conditioned: realizing them as impermanent and realizing them as suffering. The analogy of dew demonstrates realizing them as impermanent, because they do not remain for a long time. The analogy of a bubble demonstrates realizing them as suffering, because feelings are like a bubble in water, and it is said that whatever feeling there may be, that is suffering here. By way of the three types of suffering, all feelings should be understood as suffering; therein, the feeling of pain is the suffering of suffering. Those conditioned factors that are in accordance with that are also suffering by virtue of being in accordance with that. The feeling of pleasure is the suffering of change. Those phenomena that are in accordance with that are also suffering by virtue of being in accordance with that. Feelings that are neither suffering nor pleasant, and those entities that are in accordance with them, are the suffering of conditioning by virtue of the characteristic of arising and ceasing. In this way, one should view all conditioned phenomena as being possessed of suffering.Regarding that, the characteristic of realizing definitive emergence is the realization that persons and phenomena are empty. Because of that object of focus, there is definitive emergence, and thus the Bhagavan taught two types of objects of focus for definitive emergence. As it is stated in the *Ārya-samādhirāja-sūtra*:If one investigates the selflessness of phenomena individually,And having investigated them, if one meditates upon them,That is the cause for attaining the result of nirvāṇa;Any other cause will not lead to peace.All conditioned phenomena possess two types of selflessness. In this way, conditioned phenomena are of three types by the distinction of past, present, and future. Regarding that, those that are past exist only as memory; because they lack intrinsic nature, they are empty of phenomena and persons, and they have not been blessed by a self. Therefore, the analogy of a dream demonstrates the realization of those two types of selflessness. The analogy of lightning demonstrates the realization of the present, because it does not possess the nature of being a single substance or multiple substances, and thus its nature cannot be grasped. The future is of the nature of not having arrived; the analogy of a cloud demonstrates the two types of selflessness because it generates their seeds in a mind that is like the sky through the power of latent tendencies.Therefore, by all of this, it is fully taught that in this regard, a Bodhisattva should always have the intention to investigate the nature of all conditioned phenomena in that way, and should abide by means of aspiration. By teaching the realization of definitive emergence, the attainment of meditative equipoise and the supreme holding of the mind are taught. By all of these points, the profound is taught. In this verse, this is fully taught: since the root of defilement is inverted perception, and because one who engages in mental application—which involves repeatedly investigating the nature of conditioned phenomena—and others who likewise thoroughly investigate conditioned phenomena are free from inverted perception, they do not become defiled. If so, how could a Tathagata, who has meditated upon the nature of all things just as it is and is free from all webs of inverted perception, become defiled? Therefore, it should be understood that a Tathagata, having fully realized all the faults of conditioned phenomena, possesses a mind that, like a lotus, is not stained by the waters of the faults of cyclic existence; has pledged to lead all beings; acts in accordance with the result; possesses a mind endowed with great compassion; and, with the intention of accomplishing benefit and happiness for beings without delay, remains as long as cyclic existence revolves. As it is said: "In order to make the world happy, one does not abide in cyclic existence or nirvāṇa." It is also said that one dwells on the stage of looking upon all sentient beings.May the merit of this, which I have explained to the best of my ability,Which generates the Buddhas who dwell in the three times,And which is as vast as the sky,Cause me to become a Buddha who dispels the darkness of the world.The Extensive Commentary on the *Ārya-vajracchedikā* in the manner of the Middle Way, composed by the master Kamalaśīla, is completed.Translated, edited, and finalized by the Indian preceptors Mañjuśrī and Jinamitra, and the chief editor-translator, the *bande* Ye shes sde.
